name: Cinnamon-Drab
lede: Cinnamon-Drab is a muted, greyish brown, the duller cousin of Cinnamon-Buff in Robert Ridgway's 1912 color standard.

sections.title: A quieter cinnamon
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* lists Cinnamon-Drab on plate XLVI, hue 13′′′′ [1]. The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 places it in block 45, light grayish reddish brown, only 2.8 units from that block's centroid, closer than most Ridgway names come to their ISCC-NBS category [2]. The nearest named colors on file are [[beaver]], [[grey-beige]], [[dusty-cinnamon]] and [[ormond]], at 2.8, 3.7, 
The word drab itself once named a dull, undyed wool cloth before it became a color word for dullness, so Ridgway's name doubles the word: a drab, dulled cinnamon [1]. 8, 3.7, 3.9 and 4 ΔE [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of Cinnamon-Drab covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 2,015 of them, about 8.5 per cent, as photographed [3]. It is unusually common in Japanese and Chinese painting, 181 of 698 Japanese works and 127 of 635 Chinese works, and strongest of all in Nepal, 11 of 25 works [3]. It plays a highlight in 63 per cent of its appearances and a shadow in only 5 per cent [3]. These counts are museum photographs of aged, varnished paintings, and much of this brown may be the paper or silk ground rather than a painted choice [3].
